transcript.text: This is the Paper Library daily on Rare variant analysis, for Sunday, November 22.
Let's turn to rare variant analysis, with a structural variant twist.

This medRxiv preprint from the Riley lab asks whether rare copy number variants, below one percent frequency and called from short-read whole-genome sequencing in All of Us, contribute to alcohol use disorder risk.
They had about fifty-six thousand participants, roughly fifty-four hundred of them cases from health records, analyzed by ancestry group and then in a cross-ancestry meta-analysis.
The headline is mostly null. No genome-wide burden metric and no individual region of ten kilobases or more survived false discovery rate correction.

The gene-set results are interesting, though. The significant hits were almost all duplications linked to lower risk, across unrelated gene sets, so the authors read that as a general duplication dosage effect rather than pathway enrichment.

Deletions went the other way. Deletions in neurodevelopmental genes raised risk modestly, and a deletion at sixteen p twelve point one, a known neuropsychiatric locus, had an odds ratio of about two point nine, consistent across ancestries.
I'd hold that single locus loosely until it replicates. It's a preprint, the case count is modest, and short-read sequencing misses some structural variation.

The takeaway: at current biobank sample sizes, rare copy number variants seen by short-read sequencing seem to add little to alcohol use disorder liability, though the dosage signals deserve follow-up.

papers.title: Rare copy number variation in alcohol use disorder using whole-genome sequencing in the All of Us Research Program
